title: soft-decommission-and-rollback-simulations-draft
content:
Purpose:
This doc collects playbook steps and simulation notes for performing a soft node decommission (graceful eviction of inference workloads), physical GPU replacement, and fast rollback patterns. Target audience: SREs on pager, infra on-call, and solutions engineers who may need to coordinate Dedicated/Private customer capacity shifts.

Scope:
- Safe cordon/drain for nodes running latency-sensitive model shards (hosted + dedicated pools).
- Steps for hot-swap GPU replacement (on-prem + colo) and verification of KV cache warmup after rejoin.
- Cluster recovery patterns when automated backfill/autoscaler does not meet SLOs.
- Fast rollback and degradation modes: bridge-mode routing to fallback model variant, partial capacity warmstart.

Assumptions / prerequisites:
- You have cluster-admin kubectl and access to the SRE Slack channel (#sre-pager).
- Inventory and physical mapping for datacenter rack/uplink are in Hardware Tracker (vendor contact info attached to node labels).
- Replacement GPUs available in spare pool (check spare-pool index in the ops spreadsheet).
- Rolling maintenance windows pre-agreed for Dedicated customers when possible; otherwise follow emergency procedures.

Quick triage checklist (first 10 minutes):
- Confirm impact: which pools are affected? Use: curl -s "https://ops.redwood.local/api/v1/capacity?pool=gpu-xx" or check Console > Per-route latency.
- Pager details: incident severity, number of requests impacted, error classes (OOM, kernel-panic, GPU-failure).
- If node is in CrashLoop or GPU not visible: cordon immediately and mark node in inventory status=maintenance.
- Notify: post a short update in #sre-pager with node name, pool, customer-affecting? and estimated ETA for ops.

Graceful cordon & drain (soft decommission):
1) Cordon node to prevent new pods: kubectl cordon <node-name>
2) Evict pods with a conservative timeout to preserve KV caches if possible: kubectl drain <node-name> --ignore-daemonsets --delete-local-data --pod-selector='app in (inference, kvcache)' --grace-period=120 
   - Note: for latency-sensitive pods we prefer to annotate with "sre/eviction-preference=gradual" beforehand so the controller will split traffic across warm replicas.
3) Watch per-pod readiness and target pool capacity: kubectl get pods -o wide --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name>
4) If certain pods refuse eviction (stuck Terminating due to GPU-bound runtime), escalate to runtime team: @Miguel Santos. Use pre-approved emergency flag to force-delete only as last resort: kubectl delete pod <pod> --force --grace-period=0

GPU physical replacement (data center process notes):
- Confirm node is powered down and tagged in inventory. Pull the hardware runbook for the specific chassis.
- ESD precautions, vendor torque settings, thermal paste notes in Hardware Tracker.
- After swap, boot and verify OS sees the device: lspci | grep -i nvidia
- Check driver and CUDA visibility: nvidia-smi; ensure driver version matches cluster baseline. If mismatched, use the pre-built driver bundle from s3://redwood-infra/drivers/<baseline-version>.tar.gz and follow driver-install README.
- Verify dmesg for any ECC or PCIe errors: dmesg | egrep -i 'ecc|pci'

Node rejoin and runtime checks:
1) Uncordon node: kubectl uncordon <node-name>
2) Confirm node labels and taints restored (node-role.kubernetes.io/gpu, redwood/gpu-arch, hw-serial). Reapply if missing: kubectl label node <node-name> ...
3) Check autoscaler decisions: ensure cluster-autoscaler did not create incorrect new nodes.
4) Verify inference runtime starts and registers: check runtime logs via centralized logging and /var/log/redwood/runtime.log. Search for "KV cache restore" and "model loaded" events.
5) Warmup KV cache for large sharded models: run warmup script (ops-warmup) with sample prefixes used in production. Command: /opt/redwood/bin/ops-warmup --node <node-name> --model <model-id> --prefix-set warmup-v1
6) Observe latency heatmap for 20m post-join to ensure p95 is within SLO.

Capacity add & backfill patterns (when automated paths underperform):
- If autoscaler can't provision (quotas,不足 gpu stock): trigger manual capacity-add runbook:
  a) Attach additional reserved nodes (if Dedicated) by adjusting pool config: ops-cli pool update --pool gpu-reserved-1 --add-nodes 4
  b) For hosted pools, enable overflow to secondary-region (bridge-mode): ops-cli routing create --policy overflow --source us-west-1 --target us-east-1 --model-compat-check
- For immediate relief, enable degraded-mode: ops-cli set-policy --pool <pool> --degraded true --fallback-model <smaller-quantized-variant>
- Communicate to customers and product: draft incident note with expected rollback window and potential higher latency.

Rollback & graceful degradation knobs:
- Bridge-mode routing: automatically route new requests to fallback model when queue length > threshold. Ensure model variant has compatible tokenizer and structured output.
- Token-bucket throttling: temporarily lower per-customer concurrency if queue growth indicates overload.
- Cache-only serving: disable new model loads and serve from cached prefixes only until capacity stabilizes.

Post-incident simulation findings (notes from tabletop run 2024-11-07):
- Forcing pod eviction with default grace period led to KV cache cold-start penalty (~150ms p95 per request) when concurrency was >2000 QPS. We mitigated by pre-warming 3 replicas per node before eviction in simulation.
- Autoscaler API rate limit caused 2-minute lag in new node provisioning. Workaround: reserve a 10% warm buffer in pool config for peak hours.
- Hardware vendor SLA (VendorX) responded within 90 minutes; having local spare cards reduced customer-impact window by ~60 minutes. Add vendor oncall escalation to ops runbook.

Runbook TODOs / open questions:
- Add exact ops-cli commands for our new infra policy (API v2).
- Verify whether driver hotpatching is safe for models using CUDA graph caching — test on staging.
- Decide default warmup prefixes per model family (box: roberta-family, llama-family).
- Create automated test that simulates partial-GPU failure (kill GPU device driver module) and measures fallback latency.

Communications checklist (incident comms):
- Immediate: Post to #sre-pager with node, pool, customers affected, ETA.
- 30m: Post preliminary incident update with mitigation steps taken.
- Post-resolution: Draft postmortem and link to CONFLUENCE: RB-Cluster-Recovery-Postmortem-<date>. Include telemetry snapshots (latency, errors, capacity) and action items.

Postmortem action candidates:
- Increase warm spare pool for Dedicated by 1.5x during business hours.
- Add runbook automation: auto-warmup job triggered by node uncordon.
- Improve autoscaler backoff strategy to avoid hitting rate-limit windows.

Appendix: quick commands
- cordon: kubectl cordon <node-name>
- drain soft: kubectl drain <node-name> --pod-selector='app in (inference,kvcache)' --grace-period=120 --delete-local-data
- force delete pod: kubectl delete pod <pod> --force --grace-period=0
- show pods on node: kubectl get pods --field-selector spec.nodeName=<node-name> -o wide
- check GPU: ssh <node> sudo nvidia-smi -q | head -n 40

Hardware contacts & escalation
- VendorX (primary spares): vendorx-support@vendorx.com, oncall: +1-555-0199, eng contact: Rajiv Mehta
- Colo ops: colo-west@redwood.com (pager: +1-555-0188)

Notes to self:
- Keep this doc lean; pull detailed physical swap steps into Hardware Tracker and link.
- Run a drill next quarter specifically for cross-region overflow routing to validate model-compat checks.

Related artifacts and past incidents:
- INFRA-3421 (2024-11): live incident where node GPU ECC fault triggered cascade evictions — review linked postmortem.
- GH PR #878: autoscaler backoff tuning (staging only).

Unresolved:
- Does enabling bridge-mode upstream require a dedicated routing lane for high-priority customers?
- Add runbook section for on-prem private deployments where network isolation complicates warmup scripts.

End of draft.
